steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The last storm of autumn arrived without warning.

Elias felt it first as a pressure in his bones, a dense ache in his wrists and shoulders that rose with the air. The sky had been a flat pewter all afternoon, the sea unnaturally smooth, like oiled glass. By dusk the horizon vanished; sea and sky fused into a single dark mass, and the wind began to test the seams of the lighthouse.

He lit the lantern early.

Once, the lamp had been a wide, hungry flame that needed coaxing and oil and hands that knew its moods. In its place now stood an LED array, efficient and tireless, pulsing a coded pattern into the gathering gloom. Still, Elias climbed the spiral stairs the way he always had, palm along the stone so worn it felt almost soft. He checked the fixtures, wiped a nonexistent smudge from the lens, and stood watching his own light strike the invisible water far below.

On the wall beside the window, in a cheap wooden frame, was a photograph gone slightly sun-bleached: a younger Elias in the same tower, arms thrown around two children who each held a worn life ring like a crown. Their mother had taken the picture the summer before the last ferry stopped coming.

The radio crackled to life as he descended.

“… repeat, all small craft advisory. Gale-force winds and heavy swell expected within—”

He turned the volume down. The sea speaking in its own language on the rocks below was warning enough. The lighthouse shuddered as a larger wave struck, a hollow boom that lived in the ribs.

Elias made tea, the way he always did when weather came in. The kettle rattled on the old gas stove, a nervous cicada. On the table lay the logbook, its pages filled with years of neat, meticulous script. He wrote the date, the time, and, beneath the weather entry, a small note:

Last storm of the season. Last storm.

They had told him in July, over the harbor master’s polished desk, that the lighthouse would be automated fully by winter. No keeper required. Satellite feeds, remote monitoring, redundancies upon redundancies. Safe, modern, efficient. Elias had nodded, hat twisting in his hands.

“We’ll keep the building,” they’d said. “Maybe a museum. You could come back for tours, if you like.”

He had smiled, because no one liked awkward silences. “We’ll see,” he’d replied.

The first lash of rain came as a whisper, then a swarm, hurling itself against the glass with rising fury. The tower creaked, a living timber ship rising and falling with each blast. Elias carried his mug up to the watch room and settled into the worn chair beneath the lantern, its cushions molded to the shape of him over decades.

He liked storms. They drew the world in close. Land, sky, sea—everything reduced to the immediate and the essential: light against dark, sound against silence.

Through the roar, a different note slipped in—a strained, distant engine, too high, too irregular. He froze, mug halfway to his lips.

The binoculars hung from their hook by the window. He pressed the cold metal to his face and scanned the heaving black. For tense seconds there was nothing but the wild spray thrown back by his own searchlight.

Then he saw it: a small boat, little more than a smudge of white beneath his beam, climbing one gray wave, vanishing into the trough of the next. Far too close to the teeth of the rocks.

Elias set the mug down without looking, tea slopping quiet circles over the rim. His hands moved as if someone else had given them their orders years ago and they had been waiting for the command to activate again. He flicked the foghorn controls, adjusted the rotation of the beam to linger longer on the danger zone, and grabbed the radio handset.

“Vessel south-southwest of Northwick Light, this is Northwick Light. Come in.”

For a moment there was nothing. Only the wet roar of the world.

Then, through the static, a thin, frightened voice: “This is the *Marigold*. Engine’s failing. I—I can’t see a thing. Are we close to shore?”

“Too close,” Elias said. His voice, to his own ears, was calm, almost bored. “You’re near the outer reef. Can you steer?”

A pause. “Some. The wheel’s… it’s hard.”

“Good. Listen carefully. Keep my light on your starboard side. Do you understand starboard?”

“Yes. Right.” The voice was trying, tethered to panic by a thread of stubborn.

“Right,” Elias confirmed. “You’re going to angle out, away from the sound of the waves hitting rock. Can you hear them?”

“They’re everywhere.”

“Listen,” he said, and felt the peculiar stillness that came when the rest of the world demanded attention. The tower shook again. He waited, counting silently.

“There,” the voice said. “On my left. Louder.”

“That’s the shore,” Elias said. “Turn your bow a little to the right, into the swell. Do not let your nose drift left. Keep my light in sight. I’ll hold the beam on you.”

He adjusted the rotation manually, muscles remembering the resistance of the old mechanism, although now it moved with an electric hum. The light lingered, a slow, pale hand reaching out for the flailing boat.

“Northwick Light, the Coast Guard has our position, ETA twenty minutes,” came another voice, firm and clipped, sliding into the frequency.

“Understood,” Elias replied, eyes never leaving the dance of white in the dark. “They don’t have twenty minutes if they keep their current heading.”

For ten minutes, he talked the *Marigold* through the storm, his words a narrow bridge laid plank by plank. He told them when to push the engine harder despite its protests, when to ease and let the wave carry them. He spoke as he had once spoken to his own children when they’d been small and frightened of thunder: not denying the danger, but making space around it.

When the first flash of a Coast Guard cutter’s searchlight carved a second blade through the rain, Elias stepped back from the glass. The *Marigold* was still upright, that scrap of white now safely farther out, turning slowly toward rescue.

“Northwick Light, this is Coast Guard cutter *Hawthorn*. We have them,” came over the radio. “Nice work up there. Didn’t know anyone still manned that light.”

Elias allowed himself a small, private smile. “For tonight,” he said. “Northwick Light standing by.”

He hung the handset and, after a moment, turned off the manual override. The lighthouse resumed its programmed sweep, precise and indifferent.

The storm battered at the glass for another hour, then began to move on, its anger spent inland. By midnight, only a hard rain remained, an insistent tapping like fingers on a door. The sea below had gone from claws to heavy fists, still dangerous but predictable.

In the quiet that followed, Elias went back downstairs. He wiped the cooled ring of tea from the table and opened the logbook again.

Assisted *Marigold* through reef line. No casualties.

His handwriting shook slightly at the tail of the last letter. He stared at the sentence for a while, at the way the ink bled minutely into the paper fibers. When the younger man from the harbor office came in the morning with the forms and the final key exchange, this would be the last thing written in the book.

He closed it gently and slid it into his bag.

Later, near dawn, he stepped outside onto the narrow gallery that wrapped the tower. The air was sharp and clean, all the old salt smell scrubbed bright by the storm. Clouds tore slowly open in the east, stained a reluctant silver. The sea, calmed to a long, weary roll, caught the light in scattered shards.

For the first time in thirty-eight years, he looked at the lighthouse not as something he was inside of, but as a place that might no longer require him. Stone, glass, steel, and wire, standing on its shoulder of rock with the same stern patience it had always had.

Inside, the mechanisms would continue: circuits waking and dimming in sequence, lenses turning their measured arcs, messages pulsing outward like a heart that did not know it had been left alone.

Yet out there, beyond the visible line, small boats would still struggle. People would still misjudge weather and distance; engines would still fail in the worst possible places. The world would continue to need light, even if it forgot the hands that lit it.

Elias rested one hand on the painted iron rail.

“You’ll manage,” he said, not sure whether he spoke to the tower, the sea, or himself.

Behind him, the automated lamp completed its cycle and, right on time, blinked its pattern into the thinning dark: a code the passing ships could read without ever knowing who had once stood here, night after night, watching.

Down in the harbor, many miles away, the family from the *Marigold* would be stepping onto solid ground, legs weak but grateful, faces turned briefly toward the faint, still-flashing point of Northwick Light.

They would never meet the keeper. They might never learn there had been one at all.

But in his logbook, tucked now in the bottom of his bag, the ink of this night was drying. It would travel with him inland, away from the reach of the waves, a small, private record that once, when the storm closed around them, a lone, stubborn man in an old stone tower answered the dark, and the dark moved aside.
